newsitem.title: CANADA: Ford hopeful for deal with Canada auto union.
newsitem.headline: Ford hopeful for deal with Canada auto union.

text.p: Ford Motor Co.'s Canadian unit said on Monday it was optimistic it could strike a tentative deal with the Canadian Auto Workers union before a Nov. 6 strike deadline set by the union.

"I'm optimistic that we can get it done," Ford Canada chief negotiator Donald McKenzie told reporters after the opening of bargaining between the two sides. "We have basically 10 days, nine when we start tomorrow. I think that is ample time to do what we have to do."
On Monday, the CAW, which represents 11,690 unionized Ford workers in Canada, set a strike deadline of 7 P.M. EST (midnight GMT) on Nov. 6 for Ford.

Contract talks between Ford and Canada's largest private sector union began in earnest at a downtown Toronto hotel just days after a deal was reached to end a 20-day strike by 26,000 CAW members at General Motors Corp.'s Canadian operations.

CAW President Buzz Hargrove told reporters he intends to hold North America's second-largest automaker to the pattern agreement forged during talks with Chrysler Corp. and begrudgingly accepted by GM.

"I outlined the terms of the pattern settlement at Chrysler that was agreed to by General Motors and informed Mr. McKenzie that we expected to do no less here," Hargrove said. "We hope we can do that without a strike."
The two sides are expected to face off over work standards and health and safety issues.

The CAW entrenched minimum employment standards, including the right to refuse unsafe work, in the pattern agreement reached with Chrysler in an effort to block changes in workplace law by Ontario's Conservative government.
Ford has said it would like to see a narrowing of the circumstances where a worker has the right to refuse work, to prevent what it sees as a misuse of the clause.

McKenzie declined to specify when or where Ford was experiencing the problem, but he said it arose from workers "using the right to refuse for issues that are really not health and safety issues, (rather as) attempts to frustrate productivity improvements."
He said issues that held up a settlement at GM, including contracting out work, known as outsourcing, were less of an issue at Ford.
Hargrove said he was surprised by the tough stand taken by McKenzie against the pattern deal, but was taking it in stride.

"We started off, I think, on a very tough note, with Mr. McKenzie saying he had no intention of tabling any offer early, that we had to get all local agreements settled prior to any economic offer coming down ... (and that) he wasn't very fond of the pattern, period," said Hargrove.
"I'm hoping he's simply trying to stake out some ground here ... I'm not going to get excited about it this morning."

During the GM talks, the company presented its economic offer just hours before a strike deadline and well before local issues were settled. The eventual deal at GM was delayed by hang-ups over overtime, a local issue.

Ford Canada's major operations include a Windsor, Ontario, plant that supplies truck engines for the bulk of Ford's North American operations, a truck and van assembly plant in Oakville, Ontario, and a car assembly plant in St. Thomas, Ontario.
